Give generously and continue doing good (verses 1–6)

Solomon calls people who possess wealth to do good to others.

Give generously, even when it seems that what you give has been thrown away or lost.

Help many people.

Do not use the good you have already done as an excuse for refusing further opportunities to help.

Such generosity is not wasted but wisely invested.

We should expect that difficult times will sometimes come, since human beings are born to trouble.

That is one reason to do good while we are prosperous.

Riches cannot truly benefit us if we refuse to use them for the good of others.

Every person should labor to become a blessing in the community where God's Providence has placed them.

Wherever we live, there is useful work for us if our hearts are willing.

But if we magnify every small obstacle, invent objections and imagine terrible hardships, we will never begin the work, much less finish it.

Winds and clouds of trouble are in God's hands.

He uses them to test us.

His work will fulfill his word, whether or not we can see how.

We may trust the Lord to provide for us without constant anxious and distressing worry.

Do not grow tired of doing good.

At the proper time, God's time, you will reap (Galatians 6:9).

Young people should prepare for death and eternity (verses 7–10)

Life is sweet to people who reject God because the present world is their only portion.

Life is also sweet to godly people because it allows them to prepare for something far better.

In that sense, life is sweet to all.

Yet even when life seems most pleasant, we should remember death is approaching.

Solomon speaks particularly to young people.

They long to pursue many pleasures.

He challenges them: follow those desires if you wish, but remember that God will bring you into judgment.

How many young people indulge every appetite and rush toward destructive pleasures!

God records their sinful thoughts and desires, their idle words and their wicked speech.

Those who want to escape remorse and terror, possess comfort and hope near death, and avoid lasting misery must recognize the vanity of sinful pleasures in youth.

Henry emphasizes that Solomon is condemning sinful pleasures, not legitimate joy.

His goal is to lead the young toward purer and lasting happiness.

Solomon does not speak out of envy because he is too old to share in youthful amusement.

He speaks, in Henry's account, as someone rescued through a remarkable act of divine mercy from a dangerous course that few people escape.

He wants young people not to repeat his experience.

If you desire genuine happiness now and lasting happiness afterward, remember your Creator during your youth.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.11.1-Eccl.11.6]
Chapter 11
Exhortation to liberality. (Eccl. 11:1-6) An admonition to prepare for death, and to young persons to be religious. (Eccl. 11:7-10)
Verses 1-6 Solomon presses the rich to do good to others. Give freely, though it may seem thrown away and lost. Give to many. Excuse not thyself with the good thou hast done, from the good thou hast further to do. It is not lost, but well laid out. We have reason to expect evil, for we are born to trouble; it is wisdom to do good in the day of prosperity. Riches cannot profit us, if we do not benefit others. Every man must labour to be a blessing to that place where the providence of God casts him. Wherever we are, we may find good work to do, if we have but hearts to do it. If we magnify every little difficulty, start objections, and fancy hardships, we shall never go on, much less go through with our work. Winds and clouds of tribulation are, in God's hands, designed to try us. God's work shall agree with his word, whether we see it or not. And we may well trust God to provide for us, without our anxious, disquieting cares. Be not weary in well-doing, for in due season, in God's time, you shall reap, Gal. 6:9.
[Eccl.11.7-Eccl.11.10]
Verses 7-10 Life is sweet to bad men, because they have their portion in this life; it is sweet to good men, because it is the time of preparation for a better; it is sweet to all. Here is a caution to think of death, even when life is most sweet. Solomon makes an effecting address to young persons. They would desire opportunity to pursue every pleasure. Then follow your desires, but be assured that God will call you into judgment. How many give loose to every appetite, and rush into every vicious pleasure! But God registers every one of their sinful thoughts and desires, their idle words and wicked words. If they would avoid remorse and terror, if they would have hope and comfort on a dying bed, if they would escape misery here and hereafter, let them remember the vanity of youthful pleasures. That Solomon means to condemn the pleasures of sin is evident. His object is to draw the young to purer and more lasting joys. This is not the language of one grudging youthful pleasures, because he can no longer partake of them; but of one who has, by a miracle of mercy, been brought back in safety. He would persuade the young from trying a course whence so few return. If the young would live a life of true happiness, if they would secure happiness hereafter, let them remember their Creator in the days of their youth.

Remember your Creator before old age (verses 1–7)

Remember the sins you have committed against your Creator.

Repent and seek his forgiveness.

Remember also the duties you owe him and begin fulfilling them, looking to him for grace and strength.

Do this early in life, when the body is strong and the mind active.

Someone who reaches old age with the painful memory of a wasted life may finally abandon sinful pleasure only because it has become impossible to enjoy.

When such a person says, “I no longer find pleasure in these things,” sincerity in renouncing sin can reasonably be questioned.

Solomon then gives a figurative description of old age and its infirmities.

Some details of the figures are difficult to interpret.

But their central meaning is clear: the ordinary disabilities of old age often bring great discomfort.

Henry reads verses 2–5 as images of weaknesses commonly accompanying advancing age, and verse 6 as an image of what happens at the hour of death.

If sin had not entered the world, these weaknesses would not have appeared.

People who are old therefore have special reason to reflect upon the evil of sin.

Vanity, true religion and final judgment (verses 8–14)

Solomon repeats the central statement of his preaching:

“Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!”

He speaks as someone who has paid dearly to learn how empty the world is.

Earthly possessions and accomplishments cannot free people from the burden of sin.

Because Solomon understood the worth of souls, he considered carefully the words he spoke and wrote.

Truthful words will always be fitting and valuable.

God's truths resemble goads, urging on those who grow lazy and shrink back, and nails, holding steady those who wander or become unstable.

They give the heart firmness so that we neither neglect our responsibilities nor abandon them under pressure.

The Shepherd of Israel gives inspired wisdom.

Every genuine teacher and guide receives instruction from him.

Scripture also applies the title Shepherd to the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

The prophets searched diligently to understand the time and circumstances of the sufferings of Christ and the glory that would follow, as the Spirit of Christ testified through them.

Writing many books is tiring, and human life is short.

In Solomon's time producing and reading books required still greater effort than today.

But all our studies would end in vanity if they did not bring us to this conclusion:

Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole duty of humanity.

The fear of God includes all the affections directed toward him through the Holy Spirit's work.

Terror may exist without love, and may even be accompanied by hatred.

But the gracious fear of God resembles the reverence of a loving child.

It can stand for the whole of true religion within the heart and for the obedience that flows from it.

Let us pursue the one necessary thing.

Come to Christ now as a merciful Savior, for he will soon appear as the almighty Judge, bringing to light everything hidden and exposing the intentions of every heart.

Why has God told us so plainly that all is vanity?

So that we will not deceive ourselves and destroy our souls.

God has made our duty our true good.

May his command be written within every heart:

Fear God and keep his commandments, for this concerns every human being.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.12.1-Eccl.12.7]
Chapter 12
A description of the infirmities of age. (Eccl. 12:1-7) All is vanity: also a warning of the judgment to come. (Eccl. 12:8-14)
Verses 1-7 We should remember our sins against our Creator, repent, and seek forgiveness. We should remember our duties, and set about them, looking to him for grace and strength. This should be done early, while the body is strong, and the spirits active. When a man has the pain of reviewing a misspent life, his not having given up sin and worldly vanities till he is forced to say, I have no pleasure in them, renders his sincerity very questionable. Then follows a figurative description of old age and its infirmities, which has some difficulties; but the meaning is plain, to show how uncomfortable, generally, the days of old age are. As the four verses, 2-5, are a figurative description of the infirmities that usually accompany old age, Eccl. 12:6 notices the circumstances which take place in the hour of death. If sin had not entered into the world, these infirmities would not have been known. Surely then the aged should reflect on the evil of sin.
[Eccl.12.8-Eccl.12.14]
Verses 8-14 Solomon repeats his text, VANITY OF VANITIES, ALL IS VANITY. These are the words of one that could speak by dear-bought experience of the vanity of the world, which can do nothing to ease men of the burden of sin. As he considered the worth of souls, he gave good heed to what he spake and wrote; words of truth will always be acceptable words. The truths of God are as goads to such as are dull and draw back, and nails to such as are wandering and draw aside; means to establish the heart, that we may never sit loose to our duty, nor be taken from it. The Shepherd of Israel is the Giver of inspired wisdom. Teachers and guides all receive their communications from him. The title is applied in Scripture to the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The prophets sought diligently, what, or what manner of time, the Spirit of Christ in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow. To write many books was not suited to the shortness of human life, and would be weariness to the writer, and to the reader; and then was much more so to both than it is now. All things would be vanity and vexation, except they led to this conclusion, That to fear God, and keep his commandments, is the whole of man. The fear of God includes in it all the affections of the soul towards him, which are produced by the Holy Spirit. There may be terror where there is no love, nay, where there is hatred. But this is different from the gracious fear of God, as the feelings of an affectionate child. The fear of God, is often put for the whole of true religion in the heart, and includes its practical results in the life. Let us attend to the one thing needful, and now come to him as a merciful Saviour, who will soon come as an almighty Judge, when he will bring to light the things of darkness, and manifest the counsels of all hearts. Why does God record in his word, that ALL IS VANITY, but to keep us from deceiving ourselves to our ruin? He makes our duty to be our interest. May it be graven in all our hearts. Fear God, and keep his commandments, for this is all that concerns man.
